lesson.title: Hamilton, Jefferson, and the Fight Over What the Constitution Allows
lesson.summary: The 1791 fight over Alexander Hamilton's proposed national bank forced Washington's cabinet to decide how broadly the Constitution should be read, and the argument split the government into rival political parties.
lesson.body:
In December 1790, Alexander Hamilton asked Congress to charter a Bank of the United States, modeled loosely on the Bank of England and capitalized at ten million dollars combining government and private funds. Hamilton believed a national bank could stabilize the currency, provide loans to the government and merchants, and give the young nation the kind of financial infrastructure that Britain and other established powers already possessed. Congress passed the bank bill early in 1791, but before signing it Washington asked his cabinet, including Jefferson, for written opinions on whether the bill was even constitutional.

Jefferson, still serving as Secretary of State, argued forcefully that it was not. The Constitution nowhere mentioned a power to charter corporations or banks, and Jefferson insisted that under the Tenth Amendment any power not explicitly granted to the federal government belonged to the states or the people. He warned that if Congress could invent implied powers whenever convenient, the enumerated list of powers in Article I would mean almost nothing, and the federal government could grow without any real limit.

Hamilton responded with an argument for what came to be called loose or implied construction, pointing to the Constitution's necessary and proper clause, which allowed Congress to pass laws needed to carry out its enumerated powers. Since Congress already had authority to collect taxes, borrow money, and regulate commerce, Hamilton reasoned, a bank was a reasonable and useful tool for exercising those powers even though banking itself was never named. Washington, weighing both memos, ultimately sided with Hamilton and signed the bill in February 1791, chartering the First Bank of the United States for twenty years.

The dispute mattered far beyond banking. It was the first time the executive branch had to decide how broadly to read the Constitution, and the two answers Jefferson and Hamilton gave became founding arguments for opposing approaches to federal power that recurred again and again in American history, from later national bank fights to twentieth century debates over the scope of Congress's authority. It also hardened the personal and political rivalry that had begun over Hamilton's assumption plan into an organized split.

Jefferson and Madison, alarmed at what they saw as a dangerous concentration of financial and political power in Hamilton's hands, worked with allies like the newspaper editor Philip Freneau to build a political opposition around strict construction and agrarian values. By the time Jefferson left the cabinet in 1793, the loose outlines of the Federalist and Democratic-Republican parties were visible, parties that had not existed when Washington took office and were never mentioned in the Constitution itself, but that the bank debate had done more than any other single episode to bring into being.
